entries.title: Solids
entries.alt: Particles in a solid vibrate along the direction of a travelling compression. Elastic interactions transmit the disturbance; particle spacing alone does not determine sound speed.

entries.title: Liquids
entries.alt: Water particles form alternating compressions and rarefactions. The pressure disturbance travels across the liquid. Water’s resistance to compression helps it transmit sound faster than air.

entries.title: Gases
entries.alt: Air particles form alternating high and low density regions. The pressure disturbance carries energy through the gas; the particles do not travel with the wave.

entries.title: What Is Sound Intensity?
entries.alt: Sound power, the energy transferred each second, passes through a marked area. Intensity equals power divided by area, measured in watts per square metre.

entries.title: Why Does Sound Get Quieter?
entries.alt: Concentric circles represent spherical wavefronts. Two equal-sized detector areas receive different amounts of power: the farther detector receives less because the sound spreads over a larger sphere.

entries.title: Twice the Distance, One-Fourth the Intensity
entries.alt: Doubling the distance from an ideal sound source makes the spherical surface area four times larger. With the same total sound power, intensity falls to one quarter.
